candidates.speaker: Lance Bush
candidates.proposition: Realist arguments improperly rely on disputed assumptions, whereas ordinary moral improvement can be understood without those assumptions.
candidates.attributionBasis: The turn directly continues Bush's first-person defense after Enoch comments on the tone and empirical status of Bush's position.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move identifies question-begging assumptions as Bush's principal objection and invokes moral improvement as a phenomenon his anti-realist account must preserve.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Enoch's claim that Bush's presentation relies on a misleading tone of obviousness rather than a decisive argument.

candidates.contextSummary: After discussion of popular intuitions and empirical evidence, Bush redirects attention to whether realism can argue without presupposing its disputed conclusion.

candidates.speaker: David Enoch
candidates.proposition: Subjectivist paraphrases fit ordinary moral language poorly, and Bush's effort to accommodate counterfactual moral claims concedes the realist starting point.
candidates.attributionBasis: The speaker challenges Bush's proposed explanation in the second person and articulates the realist interpretation defended throughout Enoch's turns.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This move connects linguistic evidence and counterfactual moral judgment to realism while arguing that anti-realist accommodation already accepts the central explanatory task.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Bush's attempt to explain moral improvement and counterfactual moral judgment without realist commitments.

candidates.contextSummary: Enoch answers Bush by arguing both that attitude-based paraphrases are linguistically inadequate and that accommodating stance-independent-seeming judgments places both sides in the same explanatory contest.

candidates.speaker: Lance Bush
candidates.proposition: Ordinary moral language can support subjectivist analysis at least as well as realism, and realism is not needed to explain the relevant practices.
candidates.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly rejects Enoch's linguistic claims, cites subjectivist linguistic work, and restates Bush's anti-realist explanatory position.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move directly contests realism's alleged linguistic advantage and supplies Bush's alternative diagnosis that non-naturalist realism is a socially localized academic error.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Enoch's contention that subjectivist accounts distort ordinary language and implicitly concede a realist explanatory starting point.

candidates.contextSummary: Bush denies both parts of Enoch's challenge, arguing that anti-realist semantics perform equally well and shifting the explanatory burden toward why a small academic population adopts non-naturalist realism.

candidates.speaker: David Enoch
candidates.proposition: The scarcity of explicit realist belief among the general public does not count against realism, because most people lack developed views on similarly technical questions.
candidates.attributionBasis: The speaker defends Enoch's position, invokes philosophers and quantum theory, and distinguishes substantive arguments from second-order numerical evidence.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This is the principal realist response to Bush's sociological minority argument, separating lack of an opinion from disagreement and limiting the epistemic force of head counts.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Bush's claim that the tiny and socially concentrated population of non-naturalist realists is evidence against their view.

candidates.contextSummary: Enoch compares metaethics with interpretations of quantum theory, arguing that few people possess explicit theories and that numerical disagreement is at most secondary evidence rather than a substantive objection.

candidates.speaker: Lance Bush
candidates.proposition: The epistemic challenge to realism concerns a shared causal history and unreliable philosophical methods, not a straightforward appeal to majority opinion.
candidates.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly distinguishes a causal, second-order argument from raw numbers and criticizes the methods of contemporary analytic philosophers.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The clarification supplies the mechanism needed for Bush's debunking argument: common training and methods may explain convergence without tracking objective moral truth.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Enoch's quantum-theory analogy and his objection that mere numerical minority status has no bearing on a philosophical theory.

candidates.contextSummary: Bush rejects the proposed analogy by contrasting empirically productive physical models with analytic-philosophical methods and emphasizes the causal origins of a small group's shared realist commitments.

candidates.speaker: Lance Bush
candidates.proposition: A shared psychological error could causally explain realist belief even when most other people have no view, making raw numbers only a heuristic clue.
candidates.attributionBasis: The speaker corrects Enoch's description of Bush's argument and develops Bush's hallucination-and-drug analogy in first-person terms.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This move sharpens the debunking argument by specifying how a localized causal error could undermine realism without requiring widespread explicit anti-realist belief.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Enoch's charge that Bush must count everyone without an explicit metaethical view as evidence against realism.

candidates.contextSummary: Bush clarifies that the relevant consideration is an identifiable common cause of error, illustrated by a drug-induced hallucination, while treating population size merely as an initial indicator.

candidates.speaker: David Enoch
candidates.proposition: A demonstrated debunking explanation would matter, but numerical prevalence is not even a reliable heuristic because false views can spread widely.
candidates.attributionBasis: The turn grants Bush's causal analogy while defending Enoch's distinction between genuine debunking explanations and evidence based on numbers.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The response concedes the force of a successful causal genealogy but blocks the inference from minority status, thereby narrowing the anti-realist challenge to independently supported debunking evidence.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Bush's claim that a small realist population can serve as a heuristic pointing toward a shared error-producing cause.

candidates.contextSummary: Enoch accepts that a proven causal explanation could undermine a belief but argues that either truth or error may become popular, so numerical patterns add no dependable evidential support.

candidates.speaker: Lance Bush
candidates.proposition: Standard evolutionary and disagreement objections to realism are weak, but realism remains explanatorily superfluous and less parsimonious.
candidates.attributionBasis: After correcting a verbal reversal, the speaker identifies realist replies as strong and states Bush's own explanatory-superfluity objection.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move distinguishes Bush's anti-realism from conventional attacks and gives his core comparative case: moral phenomena require no realist posit and realism explains nothing better.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: The moderator's request for additional anti-realist objections such as evolutionary debunking and peer disagreement arguments.

candidates.contextSummary: Bush declines to rely on familiar debunking or disagreement arguments, credits several realist responses, and instead locates realism's cost in explanatory redundancy and parsimony.

candidates.speaker: Lance Bush
candidates.proposition: A pragmatist account can explain moral behavior, language, and psychology descriptively, dissolving realism by rejecting the shared framework of standard metaethics.
candidates.attributionBasis: The speaker expressly identifies a classical pragmatist methodology and names Bush's resulting position as anti-realist quietism.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This is Bush's foundational positive case: realism answers no antecedent problem, while a metaphilosophical change of method dissolves the conventional realism-versus-anti-realism dispute.
candidates.contextSummary: Bush traces his method to pragmatism, ordinary-language philosophy, experimental philosophy, and cognitive science, then argues that descriptive explanation eliminates any need for realism or standard anti-realist substitutes.

candidates.speaker: David Enoch
candidates.proposition: Questions that appear intelligible have prima facie legitimacy, so quietism must provide arguments rather than dismissing difficult metaethical questions as misguided.
candidates.attributionBasis: The speaker addresses Lance by implication, invokes a methodological principle, and challenges the quietist dissolution proposed in the immediately preceding turn.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move directly resists Bush's metaphilosophical strategy by shifting the burden onto quietism to explain why apparently coherent normative questions ultimately fail to make sense.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Bush's anti-realist quietist proposal that metaphilosophical inquiry dissolves the realism question rather than answering it.

candidates.contextSummary: Enoch answers the pragmatist framework with a presumption favoring intelligible questions and argues that merely denying a sufficiently difficult question is not philosophical progress.
